2. Initial System Condition
Before launching the robot, the Jetson desktop and background services already consumed approximately 2.25-2.4 GB of the available 7.6 GB RAM, with roughly 300-360 MB swap already allocated. This idle usage was not caused by the robot stack.
Perception Stack
Launching the camera, TensorRT detector, tracker, and LiDAR obstacle-detection node increased RAM to approximately 3.2-3.3 GB. The main process-level memory consumers were:
Detector: approximately 1.1 GB RSS
Camera: approximately 320-330 MB RSS

The decision, motor-control, and watchdog nodes added only about 140-160 MB. The control stack was not the main RAM problem, although the watchdog used excessive CPU because it subscribed to full camera images.
Interaction Stack
Whisper STT, the LLM node, and TTS created the largest additional memory increase. In the earlier full-stack run, RAM stabilized around 4.7-4.8 GB. STT and the detector were the two largest processes.

During voice interaction, detector logs commonly remained between approximately 25 and 28 FPS. Temporary dips occurred during STT or scene-description activity, but the detector recovered quickly.
An important testing observation was that running ros2 topic hz on both /detections and /tracked_detections simultaneously added noticeable CPU load. Future profiling should measure one high-rate topic at a time.

The LiDAR obstacle node was printing two INFO messages on every scan. At approximately 10 Hz, this produced about 20 terminal lines per second and unnecessary string formatting, ROS logging, terminal rendering, and journal activity.

Added stats_log_interval_sec parameter with a default of 1.0 second.
Added self.last_stats_log_time = 0.0.

VECTOR AMR
Complete Project Learning Handbook
ROS 2 • Computer Vision • LiDAR • Voice AI • Embedded Control • Web Interface
A technical study guide for understanding the complete autonomous mobile robot from sensor input to physical motion.
How to use this handbook
This handbook is written as a learning document rather than a README. Read Chapters 1–4 first to understand the system, then study each node in Chapter 6. Chapters 8–11 explain the external repositories, runtime flow, performance work, and interview-level concepts.
1. Project overview
Vector is a real, hardware-deployed AMR built around ROS 2 Humble. The design is modular: sensing, perception, interaction, decision-making, safety, actuation, and browser visualization communicate through ROS topics rather than being written as one monolithic program.
1.1 What the robot can do
Capture a live CSI-camera stream and publish it as ROS images.
Run real-time YOLOv8 object detection using a TensorRT engine on the Jetson GPU.

1.1 What the robot can do
Capture a live CSI-camera stream and publish it as ROS images.
Run real-time YOLOv8 object detection using a TensorRT engine on the Jetson GPU.
Track detected objects across frames and maintain track IDs.
Use a 2D RPLIDAR C1 scan to detect nearby frontal obstacles and estimate the freer side.
Follow a person, keep distance, search/roam when the person is absent, and react to obstacles.
Accept wake-word and voice commands, answer short questions through NVIDIA NIM, and describe the camera scene with a vision-language model.
Generate local speech with Piper TTS and coordinate STT muting while the robot is speaking.
Send differential left/right motor commands to an ESP32-C3 over USB serial.
Read and publish battery status.
Expose robot state and camera video to a browser dashboard through rosbridge and web_video_server.
Watch critical subsystems through a watchdog and force a safety stop when required.

2. Hardware handbook
2.1 Camera pipeline
The CSI camera uses NVIDIA's Jetson multimedia path. The working GStreamer chain is conceptually: nvarguscamerasrc → nvvidconv → videoconvert → appsink. Capture was configured at 1920×1080 @ 30 FPS and converted to a 640×480 BGR working frame. appsink uses drop=true and sync=false so old frames are discarded rather than building latency.
Camera calibration was performed with an 8×6 chessboard and 0.025 m square size. A representative intrinsic matrix recorded during the project was approximately K=[489.7,0,317.46; 0,654.72,252.84; 0,0,1].
2.2 Differential drive
The four motors are electrically/logically grouped into a left side and a right side.

recorded during the project was approximately K=[489.7,0,317.46; 0,654.72,252.84; 0,0,1].
2.2 Differential drive
The four motors are electrically/logically grouped into a left side and a right side. ROS publishes a Twist command; the motor-control node converts linear/angular intent into left/right PWM values in approximately −255…255 and sends a compact serial message to the ESP32. Equal positive PWM drives forward; unequal values turn; opposite signs rotate in place.

5. End-to-end data flow
5.1 Person-following path
Camera → /camera/image_raw → YOLO TensorRT detector → /detections → tracker → /tracked_detections → decision node → /cmd_vel → motor-control node → USB serial → ESP32 → BTS7960 → motors.
5.2 Obstacle path
RPLIDAR C1 → rplidar_node → /scan → obstacle_detection_node → /obstacle_detected + /front_distance + /free_direction → decision node → safer /cmd_vel.
5.3 Voice conversation path
USB microphone → STT → /voice_command → LLM routing → NVIDIA NIM (when needed) → /llm_response → Piper TTS → Bluetooth speaker. TTS status is also used to prevent the microphone from transcribing the robot's own speech.
5.4 Vision-question path

→ NVIDIA NIM (when needed) → /llm_response → Piper TTS → Bluetooth speaker. TTS status is also used to prevent the microphone from transcribing the robot's own speech.
5.4 Vision-question path
Voice command such as “what do you see?” → STT → LLM node recognizes a scene-description intent → copies latest camera frame → ROS Image to OpenCV → resize/JPEG/base64 → NVIDIA vision model → short text → /llm_response → Piper → speaker.
6. Detailed node-by-node handbook
6.1 camera_node
Camera acquisition and ROS publishing
Owns the Jetson CSI/GStreamer camera pipeline and continuously obtains the newest frame.
Publishes raw and compressed image streams plus CameraInfo.
Uses sensor-style BEST_EFFORT QoS with shallow depth for image data so latency is preferred over guaranteed delivery.
Final optimization added a lightweight ~1 Hz /camera/heartbeat tied to successful frame reception, allowing watchdog health checking without copying full images.

preferred over guaranteed delivery.
Final optimization added a lightweight ~1 Hz /camera/heartbeat tied to successful frame reception, allowing watchdog health checking without copying full images.
Key design idea: for real-time robotics, a fresh frame is usually more valuable than an old guaranteed frame.
6.2 detector_node
GPU object perception
Loads yolov8n.engine, the TensorRT-converted YOLOv8 nano model.
Uses approximately imgsz=640 and confidence threshold around 0.6 in the established configuration.
Subscribes to camera images, runs inference, converts results into Detection2DArray, and publishes /detections.
The engine is pre-warmed with a dummy input to avoid a large first-inference penalty.
Typical measured performance after optimization: roughly 26–29 FPS, with project logs commonly around 27–30 FPS and ~30–45 ms class of latency.
6.3 tracking_node
Temporal object tracking
Consumes /detections and maintains identities across consecutive frames.

6.3 tracking_node
Temporal object tracking
Consumes /detections and maintains identities across consecutive frames.
Uses a Kalman Filter with dim_x=8 and dim_z=4 to predict bounding-box motion/state.
Uses Hungarian assignment to match current detections to predicted tracks.
Publishes /tracked_detections including track ID/class/score information.
Tracking lets the decision layer reason about a continuing target rather than treating every frame as unrelated.
6.4 obstacle_detection_node
2D LiDAR interpretation
Consumes /scan from the RPLIDAR driver.
Examines a frontal angular sector (historically ~±20° around front) and compares ranges with an obstacle threshold around 0.50 m.
Publishes whether an obstacle exists, the nearest front distance, and a LEFT/RIGHT free-direction recommendation.
Compares left-side and right-side distance statistics to select the freer direction.

Publishes whether an obstacle exists, the nearest front distance, and a LEFT/RIGHT free-direction recommendation.
Compares left-side and right-side distance statistics to select the freer direction.
Logging was optimized from scan-rate spam to about one compact statistics line per second, with obstacle warnings only when state changes.
6.5 stt_node
Wake word, VAD, and speech transcription
Captures microphone audio and detects speech/silence before transcription.
Uses the lightweight English Whisper tiny.en family in a CTranslate2/faster-whisper-style pipeline; final settings included beam_size=1, best_of=1, temperature=0.0 and no_speech_threshold=0.6.
Recognizes the wake word “Vector”, gathers the following command, and publishes normalized commands on /voice_command.
Includes hallucination/repetition filtering and responsive shutdown logic.
Listens to TTS state so STT is muted while Vector is speaking, reducing feedback loops.

6.6 llm_node
Intent router + cloud text/vision intelligence
Receives /voice_command but does not send every command to an LLM. Local routing handles UI mode, battery, known robot controls, follow/explore acknowledgements, and vision triggers first.
Uses NVIDIA's OpenAI-compatible NIM endpoint. Text model: meta/llama-3.1-8b-instruct. Vision model: meta/llama-3.2-11b-vision-instruct.
Caches the latest camera frame. For vision questions it converts to OpenCV, downsizes when required, JPEG-encodes, base64-encodes, and submits one image with a short scene prompt.
The text system prompt identifies the robot as Vector and requests concise 10–15-word plain-text replies.
Rate limiting, duplicate suppression, vision cooldown, and detailed timing logs prevent request storms and help profile latency.
6.7 tts_node

Rate limiting, duplicate suppression, vision cooldown, and detailed timing logs prevent request storms and help profile latency.
6.7 tts_node
Offline voice output and robot face animation
Loads a Piper ONNX voice locally on CPU (use_cuda=False). The preserved final default is en_US-hfc_female-medium; HFC male/female medium voices are supported in the cleaned node.
Subscribes to /llm_response and /voice_command, queues speech, and publishes SPEAKING/IDLE status.
Uses a persistent sounddevice output stream instead of repeatedly opening audio hardware.
Maintains a very quiet 40 Hz keep-alive option to keep Bluetooth audio awake.
Caches fixed phrases lazily after first synthesis, publishes robot emotion, and derives normalized RMS mouth levels for lip-sync.
6.8 decision_node
Robot behaviour and motion decisions
Fuses tracked person detections, LiDAR obstacle information, free direction, and voice commands.

normalized RMS mouth levels for lip-sync.
6.8 decision_node
Robot behaviour and motion decisions
Fuses tracked person detections, LiDAR obstacle information, free direction, and voice commands.
Main behavioural concepts are FOLLOW, SEARCH/ROAM, PAUSED/stop, plus direct manual motion commands.
Person-following uses horizontal bounding-box center error relative to frame center (~320 px) to compute angular correction. A turn threshold around 60 px prevents unnecessary oscillation.
Bounding-box width is used as a simple visual distance proxy; a stop-width setting around 450 px prevents the robot from approaching too closely.
On temporary target loss it holds/reacquires for a short timeout (~2 s); in search mode it moves/turns to find a target; obstacle logic temporarily overrides normal following and chooses the freer LiDAR side.
6.9 watchdog_node
Independent safety supervision

(~2 s); in search mode it moves/turns to find a target; obstacle logic temporarily overrides normal following and chooses the freer LiDAR side.
6.9 watchdog_node
Independent safety supervision
Monitors critical liveness/state signals such as LiDAR, camera heartbeat, obstacle/front-distance, battery and cmd_vel.
Publishes /safety_stop when configured critical conditions are violated.
The watchdog is intentionally separate from decision logic: a fault in normal behaviour code should not remove the independent safety layer.
An important optimization replaced subscription to full /camera/image_raw with /camera/heartbeat, reducing DDS image-copy overhead and watchdog CPU from roughly 20–26% to about 11–17% in profiling.
6.10 motor_control_node
ROS-to-embedded actuation bridge
Subscribes to /cmd_vel and maps Twist linear/angular values into differential left/right motor commands.
Sends compact left,right PWM values over /dev/ttyACM0 at 115200 baud to the ESP32-C3.

bridge
Subscribes to /cmd_vel and maps Twist linear/angular values into differential left/right motor commands.
Sends compact left,right PWM values over /dev/ttyACM0 at 115200 baud to the ESP32-C3.
Commands are constrained to the motor-control range (approximately −255…255).
Sends a stop command during shutdown so the motors are not left running when ROS exits normally.
Receives/parses battery information from the microcontroller path and publishes /battery_status.
7. Behaviour logic
7.1 Why bounding-box width works for distance keeping
No monocular depth model was required. For the same person, a larger bounding box generally means the person occupies more of the image and is therefore closer. This is not metric depth, but it is cheap and adequate for a follow/stop heuristic. A future encoder/depth/SLAM system could replace this heuristic with metric distance.

8. External repositories used by the project
8.1 SLAMTEC RPLIDAR ROS 2 driver
The project uses a SLAMTEC ROS driver to turn the RPLIDAR C1 serial data stream into standard ROS LaserScan messages. The final runtime process appears as rplidar_node and publishes /scan. The driver is external code and is predominantly C/C++, so there was no need to rewrite the hardware protocol in Python.
For ROS 2, SLAMTEC's current dedicated repository is sllidar_ros2. It includes C1 launch support (for example, view_sllidar_c1_launch.py). The older Slamtec/rplidar_ros repository is the long-standing RPLIDAR ROS package and also documents C1 support. In the handbook, treat the driver as the hardware-abstraction layer: your obstacle node should consume /scan and remain independent of the low-level serial protocol.
Repository: https://github.com/Slamtec/sllidar_ros2

What the LiDAR driver does for us
Opens/configures the LiDAR communication interface.
Starts scanning and decodes SLAMTEC scan packets.
Converts polar samples into sensor_msgs/LaserScan.
Publishes standardized ranges/angles so the rest of the robot is vendor-independent.
Handles device-specific details such as baud rate and scan modes.
8.2 RobotWebTools web_video_server
web_video_server is an external RobotWebTools ROS package used to expose ROS image topics through HTTP. Instead of implementing MJPEG/H.264 streaming ourselves, the dashboard can request the camera topic from this server. It supports ROS 2 Humble+, multiple stream formats, snapshots, QoS selection, resizing, and quality controls.

Repository: https://github.com/RobotWebTools/web_video_server
Default HTTP port is commonly 8080.
Can stream raw ROS image topics as MJPEG, VP8, VP9, H264, PNG, or ROS-compressed streams.
The project intentionally left this cloned component unchanged because it already worked correctly.
This separation is useful: the camera node only publishes ROS images; the web-video component is responsible for HTTP delivery.
8.3 rosbridge_suite
rosbridge_suite provides the browser-facing JSON/WebSocket bridge. The rosbridge_server package exposes ROS publishers, subscribers and related functionality through WebSockets. This is what allows JavaScript in the dashboard to exchange ROS messages without running a native ROS client in the browser.
Repository: https://github.com/RobotWebTools/rosbridge_suite

9. Web dashboard and robot face
The browser interface combines two communication paths: rosbridge for lightweight ROS state/control messages and web_video_server for camera imagery. The dashboard includes face/vision controls, audio ON/OFF, fullscreen/close controls, and the camera feed. Voice commands can also switch face/vision UI modes through /robot_ui_mode.

10. Bringup, Docker, and repository organization
The deployed system is launched from robot_bringup, with the final process listing showing ros2 launch robot_bringup params_my_robot.launch.py. The stack runs in the Jetson ROS 2 Docker environment. A start_robot.sh wrapper was used to enter/execute the container, source the workspace, set performance-related environment variables, and launch the robot.
10.1 Key runtime environment
Base history includes dustynv/l4t-pytorch:r36.4.0 and ROS 2 Humble installation/integration.
Jetson software recorded CUDA 12.6 and PyTorch 2.6.0+cu126 with CUDA available.
YOLO inference uses TensorRT rather than ONNX Runtime GPU.
Thread limits added before launch: OMP_NUM_THREADS=1, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1, MKL_NUM_THREADS=1, NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS=1.

11. Performance and optimization lessons
11.1 The three highest-value optimizations
Limit OpenMP/BLAS worker threads. Multiple Python/ML processes creating large thread pools caused contention, memory overhead, and unstable scheduling.
Do not send full images to nodes that only need liveness. /camera/heartbeat removed unnecessary DDS image handling from the watchdog.
Throttle high-frequency logs. LiDAR statistics at scan rate created avoidable formatting, terminal, and journaling work.
11.2 Profiling caution
Running ros2 topic hz on multiple high-rate topics at the same time adds its own CPU/DDS workload.

at scan rate created avoidable formatting, terminal, and journaling work.
11.2 Profiling caution
Running ros2 topic hz on multiple high-rate topics at the same time adds its own CPU/DDS workload. Measure one important high-rate stream at a time when trying to understand the robot's real performance.
12. Important engineering decisions and lessons
12.1 What is not SLAM yet
The current robot is reactive/autonomous but not map-based. It does not yet maintain a global occupancy map, localize itself on that map, plan a global path, or use wheel-encoder odometry. Search/roam and obstacle avoidance are behaviour logic, not SLAM or Navigation2.
12.2 Natural V2 path
A future encoder-equipped chassis can retain much of this stack while adding wheel odometry, TF frames, SLAM Toolbox, localization, and Navigation2. The current camera/YOLO/interaction/web layers can remain useful above that navigation foundation.

CHAPTER 1
Interview-ready project overview
What the robot is, what it does, and how to explain it clearly.
1.1 One-sentence description
1.2 30-second answer
The robot is a modular ROS 2 Humble system running on a Jetson Orin Nano. A CSI camera feeds a TensorRT YOLO pose detector and a SORT-style tracker; an RPLIDAR C1 provides 2D obstacle ranges. A decision node combines the tracked person, LiDAR state and voice commands to publish /cmd_vel. A separate watchdog can independently force an emergency stop.

RPLIDAR C1 provides 2D obstacle ranges. A decision node combines the tracked person, LiDAR state and voice commands to publish /cmd_vel. A separate watchdog can independently force an emergency stop. The motor-control node converts Twist commands into signed PWM values and sends them by USB serial to an ESP32-C3, which drives two BTS7960 motor-driver modules. 3.4 Why topics instead of one monolithic program
ROS 2 topics decouple producers and consumers. Camera capture does not need to know whether the image goes to the detector, LLM or web stream. The decision node can be changed without rewriting the motor firmware. The watchdog can observe the same raw signals independently. This modularity improves debugging, replacement, reuse and fault isolation, at the cost of DDS serialization/transport overhead and more distributed state to reason about.
3.5 QoS choices
High-rate sensor streams use a “freshness over guaranteed delivery” philosophy. Camera image subscriptions commonly use the ROS sensor-data profile (BEST_EFFORT and shallow history) so a slow consumer does not demand retransmission of old frames. Lower-rate control/state topics use reliable queue-based profiles.

Interviewers may ask about QoS compatibility: a publisher/subscriber pair with incompatible reliability/durability settings may exchange no data even if the topic name and type match.

Detector: a latest-frame slot plus worker thread prevents a backlog of images; old frames are replaced.

For every predicted track and new detection, the node calculates IoU. It converts that similarity into a cost and uses the Hungarian algorithm to compute a one-to-one assignment. 5.4 obstacle_detection_node - LiDAR sectors and hysteresis
The obstacle node does not build a map. It is a reactive local perception component. It walks through each LaserScan sample, converts the array index to an angle, rotates it into a front-centered coordinate using front_center_angle_deg=180, and collects front/left/right sector ranges.
Why direction lock was added
A noisy scene can make left_avg and right_avg alternate around the decision boundary every scan. If the robot immediately obeys each new result, it can oscillate left-right instead of escaping. The current code chooses avoidance_direction when the obstacle is first detected and holds that direction until the obstacle state clears. This is temporal hysteresis/commitment on top of the distance hysteresis.

7.1 decision_node - behavior state machine
The decision node is the high-level behavior coordinator. It fuses tracked detections, obstacle state, front distance, freer direction, normalized voice commands, audio mode and emergency-stop state. It is not a path planner and does not maintain a global map.
Wake/command behavior
On WAKE_WORD_DETECTED the node stores the prior mode/follow flag and stops. STOP remains stopped. FOLLOW_PERSON/SEARCH enables following. Direct LEFT/RIGHT/FORWARD/BACKWARD starts a timed maneuver and then returns to the saved mode. DESCRIBE_SCENE/BATTERY_STATUS and normal conversation restore the pre-wake behavior because those commands do not require a motion-mode change.

Obstacle priority inside decision
If obstacle_detected is true, obstacle avoidance takes priority over following/roaming. The current behavior initially stops, then rotates toward the /free_direction. The obstacle node’s direction lock prevents the selected side from flipping every scan. When the obstacle clears, normal behavior resumes.
Person-following algorithm
The decision node chooses a tracked person. It tries to keep the same track ID; if that ID is unavailable it can select the largest person box as the next target. Horizontal image error is center_x(target) - 320. Angular velocity is proportional to the negative error. Box width acts as a cheap distance proxy: a wide box implies the same person is nearer.

7.2 watchdog_node - independent safety supervisor
The watchdog is deliberately separate from decision logic. Safety should not disappear if the decision node has a bug. It monitors data liveness, raw LiDAR proximity and battery state. A set of active fault reasons determines whether emergency stop is asserted.
Why it also publishes zero /cmd_vel
The watchdog publishes /emergency_stop for the decision node, but it also directly publishes a zero Twist as a failsafe. This is defense in depth: even if normal decision cooperation is delayed or broken, a safety process can still send a stop command down the actuation path.

Multiple faults can exist at once. The code stores them in active_reasons and only releases emergency stop when every active condition is cleared. 8.3 BTS7960 direction principle
Each side has two PWM inputs. A positive signed command drives RPWM and sets LPWM to zero; a negative command sets RPWM to zero and drives LPWM with the absolute magnitude. Zero clears both. The enable pins are held HIGH so the H-bridge accepts PWM commands.

11.2 Thread oversubscription
Several Python/ML libraries can each create OpenMP/BLAS worker pools. In a multi-process ROS stack on a six-core Jetson, every process creating many compute threads caused contention, context switching, extra memory and unpredictable callback scheduling. Setting OMP_NUM_THREADS, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS and NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS to 1 at stack launch produced a large stability improvement.

When left and right free-space estimates changed slightly from scan to scan, the robot could alternate turn direction instead of committing to an escape. 11.8 Person-follow collision lesson
Pure image-space person following is not sufficient collision avoidance. The person target can encourage forward motion while a table or other non-person object lies in the path. A stronger V2 would fuse navigation costmaps/depth and wheel odometry rather than relying on a single follow heuristic.

13.1 ROS 2 publisher/subscriber model
A publisher writes typed messages to a named topic. A subscriber receives compatible messages. DDS handles discovery and transport. The nodes do not call each other directly for streaming data, so producers and consumers can evolve independently.
13.2 Twist message
geometry_msgs/Twist contains linear and angular velocity vectors. For a planar mobile robot, this project primarily uses linear.x for forward/backward intent and angular.z for yaw/turn intent.
13.3 Sensor QoS

contains linear and angular velocity vectors. For a planar mobile robot, this project primarily uses linear.x for forward/backward intent and angular.z for yaw/turn intent.
13.3 Sensor QoS
BEST_EFFORT can drop samples instead of retrying them. For a high-rate camera, a newer frame can be more useful than retransmitting an old frame. Reliable delivery is more useful for low-rate control/state where missing a transition matters.
13.4 TensorRT
TensorRT optimizes a trained network for inference on NVIDIA GPUs and serializes the optimized execution plan as an engine. It is a deployment/inference technology, not a training framework.
13.5 IoU
Intersection over Union = area(intersection) / area(union). It ranges from 0 to 1 and measures how much two bounding boxes overlap. The tracker uses it as an association similarity.
13.6 Hungarian algorithm

over Union = area(intersection) / area(union). It ranges from 0 to 1 and measures how much two bounding boxes overlap. The tracker uses it as an association similarity.
13.6 Hungarian algorithm
Given a cost matrix between predicted tracks and detections, the Hungarian algorithm computes a globally optimal one-to-one assignment for the matrix objective rather than greedily matching each object independently.
13.7 Kalman filter
A recursive estimator alternates predict and update. Prediction uses a motion model; update uses the new measurement weighted according to uncertainty. It provides both an estimated state and covariance.
13.8 Hysteresis
Use different thresholds for entering and leaving a state. With obstacle trigger at 0.50 m and clear at 0.60 m, noise around 0.50 no longer causes rapid on/off switching.
13.9 Proportional steering
angular.z = -K × horizontal_error. The farther the target is from image center, the stronger the turn.

at 0.60 m, noise around 0.50 no longer causes rapid on/off switching.
13.9 Proportional steering
angular.z = -K × horizontal_error. The farther the target is from image center, the stronger the turn. A deadband near center prevents small noise from generating continuous corrections.
13.10 Open-loop vs closed-loop control
Open-loop timed PWM assumes the hardware response. Closed-loop control measures output (e.g., encoder speed/distance), calculates error against a target and adjusts commands. The current direct distance/turn maneuvers are open-loop.
13.11 Watchdog
A watchdog independently observes whether critical subsystems are alive and whether safety constraints hold. It should fail safe: if necessary information disappears, motion is inhibited rather than assumed safe.
13.12 State machine
Behavior is represented by explicit states/flags and defined transitions. This is easier to reason about than many independent callbacks writing motion commands with no priority model.

Q1. Give me the architecture of your robot.
Answer: I split it into sensing, perception, interaction, decision/safety, actuation and web layers. The main motion path is camera -> TensorRT pose detection -> tracking -> decision -> /cmd_vel -> motor bridge -> ESP32 -> BTS7960 -> motors, while LiDAR and an independent watchdog can override motion.
Q2. Why ROS 2?
Answer: I needed a modular distributed architecture where camera, perception, voice, safety and hardware could be developed and debugged independently. ROS 2 also gives standard message types, DDS discovery/QoS, launch/configuration and a large robotics ecosystem.
Q3. Why not put everything in one Python program?

and debugged independently. ROS 2 also gives standard message types, DDS discovery/QoS, launch/configuration and a large robotics ecosystem.
Q3. Why not put everything in one Python program?
Answer: It would reduce some transport overhead, but it would couple failure modes and make development/debugging harder. Separate nodes let me isolate bottlenecks, restart components, inspect topics and keep the safety watchdog independent.
Q4. Why use TensorRT?
Answer: The robot runs inference on an NVIDIA Jetson. TensorRT turns the exported network into an optimized GPU engine, which gives lower latency and higher/stabler throughput than running the training model path directly.
Q5. Is YOLO running on every frame?
Answer: The detector always keeps only the newest image available to its worker. If inference is busy, the incoming slot is replaced. This intentionally drops stale frames instead of creating latency.
Q6. Why do you need a tracker after YOLO?
Answer: YOLO detections are frame-local.

inference is busy, the incoming slot is replaced. This intentionally drops stale frames instead of creating latency.
Q6. Why do you need a tracker after YOLO?
Answer: YOLO detections are frame-local. The tracker adds temporal identity, smooth prediction through brief misses and lets the decision node maintain the same person rather than selecting an unrelated detection every frame.
Q7. Explain your tracker.
Answer: Each track has a Kalman state. I predict tracks, compute IoU against new detections, use the Hungarian assignment to find one-to-one matches, update matched tracks, create tracks for unmatched detections and age/remove unmatched tracks.
Q8. What is IoU?
Answer: Intersection area divided by union area for two boxes. I use it as the similarity for associating detections with predicted tracks.
Q9. What does the Kalman filter do here?
Answer: It predicts box state between measurements and corrects the estimate when a new detection arrives.

for associating detections with predicted tracks.
Q9. What does the Kalman filter do here?
Answer: It predicts box state between measurements and corrects the estimate when a new detection arrives. The covariance represents uncertainty, so prediction and measurement are combined systematically.
Q10. What is the Hungarian algorithm doing?
Answer: It solves the assignment problem over the track-detection cost matrix, giving a global one-to-one matching instead of independent greedy matches.
Q11. How do you detect obstacles?
Answer: I convert each LaserScan index to an angle, rotate into the robot’s physical front coordinate, collect front/left/right sectors, use the minimum front distance for obstacle state, and compare side averages to choose the freer direction.
Q12. Why is front_center_angle 180 degrees?
Answer: The physical LiDAR mounting/message convention meant its zero direction did not correspond to the chassis front.

to choose the freer direction.
Q12. Why is front_center_angle 180 degrees?
Answer: The physical LiDAR mounting/message convention meant its zero direction did not correspond to the chassis front. I verified that experimentally and explicitly rotate the scan interpretation by 180 degrees.
Q13. How did you stop left-right oscillation?
Answer: I added a direction deadband, separate detect/clear thresholds and latched the chosen avoidance direction while an obstacle event remains active. That prevents noisy scans from changing the turn side every callback.
Q14. How does person following work?
Answer: I use the tracked person box center relative to the 640-pixel image center for steering, and box width as a rough distance proxy. If the box is too large I stop; otherwise I move and steer proportionally.
Q15. Why is box width not real distance?
Answer: It depends on person size, pose and camera geometry. It is a cheap monocular heuristic, not metric depth.

otherwise I move and steer proportionally.
Q15. Why is box width not real distance?
Answer: It depends on person size, pose and camera geometry. It is a cheap monocular heuristic, not metric depth. For V2 I would prefer depth or navigation/odometry-based distance.
Q16. What happens if the target disappears?
Answer: There is a roughly 2-second reacquisition window. The robot stops during temporary loss. If the target remains absent, autonomous behavior returns to roaming/search.
Q17. How does a voice command reach the motors?
Answer: STT publishes a normalized token on /voice_command. The decision node changes state or starts a timed maneuver, publishes Twist on /cmd_vel, the motor node converts that to signed left/right PWM, and the ESP32 drives the H-bridges.
Q18. Why stop at the wake word?
Answer: The robot should not keep roaming while the user is trying to command it.

Q18. Why stop at the wake word?
Answer: The robot should not keep roaming while the user is trying to command it. I save the previous mode, publish zero velocity, process the command, and then either change behavior or restore the previous mode.
Q19. How accurate is your “move one meter” command?
Answer: It is an open-loop timed estimate: 0.25 m/s for 4 seconds. Without wheel encoders it is not guaranteed to be one meter. Encoder odometry and a closed-loop controller are the correct V2 solution.
Q20. What role does the LLM play in motion control?
Answer: It does not directly control the motors. Known robot intents are routed locally and the decision node owns motion. The LLM is for conversational responses and on-demand vision-language questions.
Q21. Why route commands locally before the LLM?
Answer: STOP, follow, UI and battery actions should be deterministic and low latency.

conversational responses and on-demand vision-language questions.
Q21. Why route commands locally before the LLM?
Answer: STOP, follow, UI and battery actions should be deterministic and low latency. Local routing also avoids unnecessary network requests, cost and variability.
Q22. Which models are local and which are remote?
Answer: YOLO pose, Whisper/faster-whisper and Piper are executed on the Jetson stack. The text and vision LLM requests use NVIDIA NIM remotely. The tracker/LiDAR/decision/watchdog are classical algorithms rather than learned models.
Q23. How does scene description work?
Answer: The LLM node caches the latest camera image. On a vision command it converts it to OpenCV, downsizes the longest side to 640 if needed, JPEG/base64 encodes it and sends one multimodal request to the NIM vision model.
Q24. How do you prevent the robot hearing itself?
Answer: TTS publishes SPEAKING/IDLE. While it is speaking, STT drains/ignores microphone audio.

sends one multimodal request to the NIM vision model.
Q24. How do you prevent the robot hearing itself?
Answer: TTS publishes SPEAKING/IDLE. While it is speaking, STT drains/ignores microphone audio. After IDLE it waits for a short echo-decay period and flushes buffered audio before listening again.
Q25. Why Piper on CPU?
Answer: TTS is intermittent and practical on CPU, while the GPU is more valuable for continuous perception. It also keeps speech local/offline.
Q26. Why use a persistent audio stream?
Answer: Repeatedly opening/closing the audio device adds latency and can be unreliable, especially with Bluetooth. A persistent output stream lets synthesis only update the playback buffer.
Q27. Why is your watchdog separate?
Answer: A safety monitor inside decision_node would share the same failure domain. A separate node observes raw/derived signals and can publish zero velocity independently if the normal behavior node fails.
Q28.

Q28. Why monitor raw /scan instead of only /front_distance?
Answer: Raw /scan gives the watchdog an independent path. If obstacle_detection_node itself fails or publishes bad/stale derived data, the watchdog can still inspect the physical LiDAR signal.
Q29. Why did you replace camera images with a heartbeat in the watchdog?
Answer: The watchdog only needs liveness. Receiving 30 FPS full images wasted DDS/Python copying and CPU. A 1 Hz heartbeat tied to successful frames preserves the safety information at a fraction of the cost.
Q30. What happens if multiple safety faults exist?
Answer: The watchdog keeps a set of active reasons. Emergency stop remains asserted until all reasons clear, so recovery of one sensor cannot accidentally release a stop caused by another fault.
Q31.

Answer: The watchdog keeps a set of active reasons. Emergency stop remains asserted until all reasons clear, so recovery of one sensor cannot accidentally release a stop caused by another fault.
Q31. How do you avoid critical-distance chatter?
Answer: Trigger at 0.28 m and clear at 0.35 m. I also require forward motion before triggering the raw-LiDAR proximity reason.
Q32. Explain /cmd_vel to motor PWM.
Answer: For normal driving, base=int(linear.x*250) and turn=int(angular.z*150). Left=base-turn, right=(base+turn)*0.9. I clamp to ±255, apply a deadzone of 15 and send the two integers to the ESP32.
Q33. Why the 0.90 right motor correction?
Answer: The four open-loop DC motors did not have perfectly matched speed. It is a simple feed-forward compensation. Encoders with closed-loop wheel-speed control would be more robust.
Q34. Why an ESP32 at all?

four open-loop DC motors did not have perfectly matched speed. It is a simple feed-forward compensation. Encoders with closed-loop wheel-speed control would be more robust.
Q34. Why an ESP32 at all?
Answer: The Jetson should handle perception and high-level logic, while the MCU provides simple deterministic GPIO/PWM/ADC hardware control and isolates Linux/ROS from driver pin timing.
Q35. What does the ESP32 receive?
Answer: A newline-terminated left,right pair of signed PWM values at 115200 baud. Positive/negative sign chooses the H-bridge direction and magnitude sets PWM duty.
Q36. How is battery status sent back?
Answer: The ESP32 reports a raw ADC sample as BATT:<raw>. The Jetson reconstructs voltage using 4095, 3.3 V and the 100k/33k divider, maps 9.0-12.6 V to a percentage and publishes /battery_status.
Q37. What is the biggest embedded safety gap?
Answer: The firmware should independently stop motors if valid serial commands stop arriving.

Q37. What is the biggest embedded safety gap?
Answer: The firmware should independently stop motors if valid serial commands stop arriving. The ROS watchdog covers the Linux stack, but an MCU communication timeout would cover Jetson/USB failure below ROS.
Q38. What was your biggest performance fix?
Answer: Limiting hidden OpenMP/BLAS threads across the multi-process stack. Oversubscription caused contention and unstable scheduling; setting those libraries to one thread per process improved RAM and detector stability.
Q39. How did you profile the robot?
Answer: I measured per-process CPU/RSS, topic rates, detector latency/FPS, tegrastats GPU/CPU/temperature/power and observed behavior under the full stack. I changed one bottleneck at a time and re-measured.
Q40. What is rosbridge versus web_video_server?
Answer: rosbridge exposes ROS messages/control to browser JavaScript over WebSocket/JSON.

stack. I changed one bottleneck at a time and re-measured.
Q40. What is rosbridge versus web_video_server?
Answer: rosbridge exposes ROS messages/control to browser JavaScript over WebSocket/JSON. web_video_server is specialized for serving ROS image topics as browser-friendly video streams.
Q41. Is this a real AMR if it has no SLAM?
Answer: It is an autonomous mobile robot in the sense that it senses, makes autonomous reactive decisions and actuates itself. It is not yet a map-based Nav2 AMR. I explicitly distinguish reactive autonomy from localization/SLAM/navigation.
Q42. What would you add first for a production-like V2?
Answer: Encoder motors and odometry, MCU command timeout, standard TF frames, IMU fusion, SLAM/localization and Nav2 costmaps/planners. Those changes would replace timed motion and reactive roaming with closed-loop navigation.
Q43. What are the failure modes of cloud LLM dependence?

SLAM/localization and Nav2 costmaps/planners. Those changes would replace timed motion and reactive roaming with closed-loop navigation.
Q43. What are the failure modes of cloud LLM dependence?
Answer: Network/API latency or outage affects conversation and scene description, but not core obstacle safety or known motion commands because those are local. That separation is deliberate.
Q44. What would you test automatically?
Answer: Unit tests for parsing/mixing/threshold state transitions, recorded rosbag regression for LiDAR and detections, integration tests for topic liveness and e-stop, and hardware-in-loop serial timeout/stop tests.
Q45. How would you make obstacle avoidance better?
Answer: Use odometry and Nav2 local costmaps/controllers, potentially fuse depth/camera semantics, and turn the current sector logic into a safety layer rather than the main navigation strategy.
Q46. How would you improve following?

costmaps/controllers, potentially fuse depth/camera semantics, and turn the current sector logic into a safety layer rather than the main navigation strategy.
Q46. How would you improve following?
Answer: Use metric target range, target re-identification if needed, a smoother controller, velocity/acceleration limits and navigation-aware collision checking rather than only image error and box width.
Q47. What did you learn from the project?
Answer: The main lesson is systems engineering: model speed alone is not enough. Coordinate frames, QoS, thread pools, stale data, feedback loops, motor mismatch, safety ownership and instrumentation all determine whether an AI robotics system works on real hardware.

This watchdog independently checks the liveness of the LiDAR, obstacle detector, tracker, camera heartbeat, and velocity-command stream. Digital Power Supply
ESP32-C3 has pin17 VDD3P3_CPU as the digital power supply pin(s) working in a voltage range of 3.0 V ~ 3.6 V.
It is recommended to add an extra 0.1 μF decoupling capacitor close to the pin(s).
Pin VDD_SPI can serve as the power supply for the external device at 3.3 V (typical value), provided by
VDD3P3_CPU via RSPI. Therefore, there will be some voltage drop from VDD3P3_CPU. When the VDD_SPI
outputs 3.3 V, it is recommended that users add a 1 μF capacitor close to VDD_SPI.
VDD_SPI can be connected to and powered by an external power supply.
When not serving as a power supply pin, VDD_SPI can be used as a regular GPIO.

Analog Power Supply
ESP32-C3’s VDDA and VDD3P3 pins are the analog power supply pins, working at 3.0 V ~ 3.6 V.
For VDD3P3, when ESP32-C3 is transmitting signals, there may be a sudden increase in the current draw, causing
power rail collapse. Therefore, it is highly recommended to add a 10 μF capacitor to the power rail, which can work
in conjunction with the 0.1 μF capacitor(s) or other capacitors.
It is suggested to add an extra 10 μF capacitor at the main power entrance. If the main power entrance is close to
VDD3P3, then the two 10 μF capacitors can be merged into one.

ESP32-C3’s CHIP_EN pin can enable the chip when it is high and reset the chip when it is low.
When ESP32-C3 uses a 3.3 V system power supply, the power rails need some time to stabilize before CHIP_EN

ESP32-C3 supports an external 32.768 kHz crystal to act as the RTC clock. The external RTC clock source enhances

• Load capacitance at both ends should be configured according to the crystal’s specification.
The parallel resistor R is used for biasing the crystal circuit (5 MΩ< R ≤10 MΩ).

RF Circuit
ESP32-C3’s RF circuit is mainly composed of three parts, the RF traces on the PCB board, the chip matching
circuit, the antenna and the antenna matching circuit. Each part should meet the following requirements:
• For the RF traces on the PCB board, 50 Ωimpedance control is required.
• For the chip matching circuit, it must be placed close to the chip. A CLC structure is preferred.
– The CLC structure is mainly used to adjust the impedance point and suppress harmonics, and
a set of LC can be added if space permits.
– The RF matching circuit is shown in Figure ESP32-C3 Schematic for RF Matching.
• For the antenna and the antenna matching circuit, to ensure radiation performance, the antenna’s characteristic
impedance must be around 50 Ω.

is shown in Figure ESP32-C3 Schematic for RF Matching.
• For the antenna and the antenna matching circuit, to ensure radiation performance, the antenna’s characteristic
impedance must be around 50 Ω. Adding a CLC matching circuit near the antenna is recommended to adjust
the antenna. However, if the available space is limited and the antenna impedance point can be guaranteed to
be 50 Ωby simulation, then there is no need to add a matching circuit near the antenna.

General Principles of PCB Layout for the Chip
It is recommended to use a four-layer PCB design:
• Layer 1 (TOP): Signal traces and components.
• Layer 2 (GND): No signal traces here to ensure a complete GND plane.
• Layer 3 (POWER): GND plane should be applied to better isolate the RF and crystal. Route power traces and
a few signal traces on this layer, provided that there is a complete GND plane under the RF and crystal.
• Layer 4 (BOTTOM): Route a few signal traces here. It is not recommended to place any components on this
layer.
A two-layer PCB design can also be used:
• Layer 1 (TOP): Signal traces and components.
• Layer 2 (BOTTOM): Do not place any components on this layer and keep traces to a minimum.

Figure ESP32-C3 Crystal Layout (without Keep-out Area on Top Layer) shows the layout for the crystal that is con-
nected to the ground through vias but there is no keep-out area on the top layer for ground isolation.
The layout of the crystal should follow the guidelines below:
• Ensure a complete GND plane for the RF, crystal, and chip.
• The crystal should be placed far from the clock pin to avoid interference on the chip. The gap should be at least
2.0 mm. It is good practice to add high-density ground vias stitching around the clock trace for better isolation.
• There should be no vias for the clock input and output traces.
• Components in series to the crystal trace should be placed close to the chip side.
• The external matching capacitors should be placed on the two sides of the crystal, preferably at the end of the
clock trace, but not connected directly to the series components.

1.4.8
USB
The USB layout should meet the following guidelines:
• Reserve space for resistors and capacitors on the USB traces close to the chip side.
• Use differential pairs and route them in parallel at equal lengths. Maintain a differential pair impedance of 90
Ω with a tolerance of ±10%.
• USB differential traces should minimize via transitions as much as possible to ensure better impedance control
and avoid signal reflections. If vias are necessary, add a pair of ground return vias at each transition point.
• Ensure there is a continuous reference layer (a ground layer is recommended) beneath the USB traces.
• Surround the USB traces with ground copper.

You can download firmware to ESP32-C3 via UART and USB.
To download via UART:
1. Before the download, make sure to set the chip or module to Joint Download Boot mode, according to Table
Boot Mode Control.
2. Power up the chip or module and check the log via the UART0 serial port. If the log shows “waiting for
download”, the chip or module has entered Joint Download Boot mode.
3. Use the Flash Download Tool to flash firmware into flash via UART.
4. After the firmware has been downloaded, pull GPIO9 high or leave it floating to make sure that the chip or
module enters SPI Boot mode.
5. Power up the chip or module again. The chip will read and execute the new firmware during initialization.
To download via USB:
1. If the flash is empty, set the chip or module to Joint Download Boot mode, according to Table Boot Mode
Control.
2. Power up the chip or module and check the log via USB serial port. If the log shows “waiting for download”

2.2
Pin Overview
The ESP32-C3 chip integrates multiple peripherals that require communication with the outside world. To keep
the chip package size reasonably small, the number of available pins has to be limited. So the only way to
route all the incoming and outgoing signals is through pin multiplexing. Pin muxing is controlled via software
programmable registers (see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter IO MUX and GPIO
Matrix).
All in all, the ESP32-C3 chip has the following types of pins:
• IO pins with the following predefined sets of functions to choose from:
– Each IO pin has predefined IO MUX functions – see Table 2-4 IO MUX Pin Functions
– Some IO pins have predefined analog functions – see Table 2-6 Analog Functions
Predefined functions means that each IO pin has a set of direct connections to certain signals from
on-chip peripherals. During run-time, the user can configure which peripheral signal from a predefined

functions means that each IO pin has a set of direct connections to certain signals from
on-chip peripherals. During run-time, the user can configure which peripheral signal from a predefined
set to connect to a certain pin at a certain time via memory mapped registers.
• Analog pins that have exclusively-dedicated analog functions – see Table 2-8 Analog Pins
• Power pins that supply power to the chip components and non-power pins – see Table 2-9 Power Pins

2.3.1
IO MUX Functions
The IO MUX allows multiple input/output signals to be connected to a single input/output pin. Each IO pin of
ESP32-C3 can be connected to one of the three signals (IO MUX functions, i.e., F0-F2), as listed in Table 2-4
IO MUX Pin Functions.
Among the three sets of signals:
• Some are routed via the GPIO Matrix (GPIO0, GPIO1, etc.), which incorporates internal signal routing
circuitry for mapping signals programmatically. It gives the pin access to almost any peripheral signals.
However, the flexibility of programmatic mapping comes at a cost as it might affect the latency of routed
signals. For details about connecting to peripheral signals via GPIO Matrix, see
ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter IO MUX and GPIO Matrix.
• Some are directly routed from certain peripherals (U0TXD, MTCK, etc.), including UART0, JTAG, SPI0/1,
and SPI2 - see Table 2-3 Peripheral Signals Routed via IO MUX.

2.3.3
Restrictions for GPIOs
All IO pins of ESP32-C3 have GPIO pin functions. However, the IO pins are multiplexed and can be configured
for different purposes based on the requirements. Some IOs have restrictions for usage. It is essential to
consider the multiplexed nature and the limitations when using these IO pins.
In tables of this chapter, the following pin functions are highlighted in red or yellow . These functions
indicate pins that require extra caution when used as GPIO / GPIO :
• IO Pins – allocated for communication with in-package flash and NOT recommended for other uses.
For details, see Section 2.6 Pin Mapping Between Chip and Flash.
• IO Pins – have one of the following important functions:
– Strapping pins – need to be at certain logic levels at startup. See Section 3 Boot Configurations.
Note:
Strapping pins are highlighted by Pin Name or configurations At Reset, instead of the pin functions.

– USB_D+/- – by default, connected to the USB Serial/JTAG Controller. To function as GPIOs, these

– JTAG interface – often used for debugging. See Table 2-3 Peripheral Signals Routed via IO MUX.
To free these pins up, the pin functions USB_D+/- of the ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual

– UART0 interface – often used for debugging. See Table 2-3 Peripheral Signals Routed via IO MUX.
– VDD_SPI – the power supply pin for flash by default, and can only be used as a GPIO pin if the flash

2.3.4
Peripheral Pin Assignment
Table 2-7 Peripheral Pin Assignment highlights which pins can be assigned to each peripheral interface
according to the following priorities:
• Priority 1 : Fixed pins connected directly to peripheral signals via IO MUX.
If a peripheral interface does not have priority 1 pins, such as UART1, it can be assigned to any GPIO pins
from priority 2 to priority 4.
• Any GPIO pins mapping to peripheral signals via GPIO Matrix, can be priority 2, 3, or 4.
– Priority 2 : GPIO pins can be freely used without restrictions.
– Priority 3 : GPIO pins should be used with caution, as they may conflict with the following
important functions described in Section 2.3.3 Restrictions for GPIOs:
* GPIO2, GPIO8, GPIO9 : Strapping pins.
* GPIO18, GPIO19 : USB Serial/JTAG interface.
* GPIO4, GPIO5, GPIO6, GPIO7 : JTAG interface.
* GPIO20, GPIO21 : UART0 interface.
* GPIO11 : The VDD_SPI pin. The power supply pin for flash by default, and can only be

: USB Serial/JTAG interface.
* GPIO4, GPIO5, GPIO6, GPIO7 : JTAG interface.
* GPIO20, GPIO21 : UART0 interface.
* GPIO11 : The VDD_SPI pin. The power supply pin for flash by default, and can only be
reconfigured as a GPIO pin if the flash is powered by an external power supply.
– Priority 4 : GPIO pins already allocated or not recommended for use, as described in Section 2.3.3
Restrictions for GPIOs:
* GPIO12, GPIO13, GPIO14, GPIO15, GPIO16, GPIO17 : SPI0/1 interface connected to the
in-package flash, or recommended for the off-package flash.
If a peripheral interface does not have priority 2 to 4 pins, such as USB Serial/JTAG, it means it can be
assigned only to priority 1 pins.

4.1.1
Microprocessor and Master
This subsection describes the core processing units within the chip and their capabilities.
4.1.1.1
High-Performance CPU
ESP32-C3 has a low-power 32-bit RISC-V single-core microprocessor with the following features:
• Four-stage pipeline that supports a clock frequency of up to 160 MHz
• RV32IMC ISA
• 32-bit multiplier and 32-bit divider
• Up to 32 vectored interrupts at seven priority levels
• Up to 8 hardware breakpoints/watchpoints
• Up to 16 PMP regions
• JTAG for debugging
For details, see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter High-Performance CPU.
4.1.1.2
GDMA Controller
ESP32-C3 has a general DMA controller (GDMA) with six independent channels, i.e. three transmit channels
and three receive channels.

Manual > Chapter High-Performance CPU.
4.1.1.2
GDMA Controller
ESP32-C3 has a general DMA controller (GDMA) with six independent channels, i.e. three transmit channels
and three receive channels. These six channels are shared by peripherals with DMA feature. The GDMA
controller implements a fixed-priority scheme among these channels, whose priority can be configured.
The GDMA controller controls data transfer using linked lists. It allows peripheral-to-memory and
memory-to-memory data transfer at a high speed. All channels can access internal RAM.
Peripherals on ESP32-C3 with DMA feature are SPI2, UHCI0, I2S, AES, SHA, and ADC.
For details, see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter GDMA Controller (DMA).

4.1.3.1
IO MUX and GPIO Matrix
ESP32-C3 has 22 or 16 GPIO pins which can be assigned various functions by configuring corresponding
registers. Besides digital signals, some GPIOs can be also used for analog functions, such as ADC.
All GPIOs have selectable internal pull-up or pull-down, or can be set to high impedance. When these GPIOs
are configured as an input, the input value can be read by software through the register. Input GPIOs can also
be set to generate edge-triggered or level-triggered CPU interrupts. All digital IO pins are bi-directional,
non-inverting and tristate, including input and output buffers with tristate control.

The IO MUX and the GPIO matrix are used to route signals from peripherals to GPIO pins. Together they

CPU Clock
The CPU clock has three possible sources:
• External main crystal clock
• Fast RC oscillator (typically about 17.5 MHz, and adjustable)
• PLL clock
The application can select the clock source from the three clocks above. The selected clock source drives
the CPU clock directly, or after division, depending on the application. Once the CPU is reset, the default
clock source would be the external main crystal clock divided by 2.
Note:
ESP32-C3 is unable to operate without an external main crystal clock.
RTC Clock
The RTC slow clock is used for RTC counter, RTC watchdog and low-power controller. It has three possible
sources:
• External low-speed (32 kHz) crystal clock
• Internal slow RC oscillator (typically about 136 kHz, and adjustable)
• Internal fast RC oscillator divided clock (derived from the fast RC oscillator divided by 256)

• Internal fast RC oscillator divided clock (derived from the fast RC oscillator divided by 256)
The RTC fast clock is used for RTC peripherals and sensor controllers. It has two possible sources:
• External main crystal clock divided by 2
• Internal fast RC oscillator divide-by-N clock (typically about 17.5 MHz, and adjustable)

System Timer
ESP32-C3 integrates a 52-bit system timer, which has two 52-bit counters and three comparators. The system
timer has the following features:
• Counters with a fixed clock frequency of 16 MHz
• Three types of independent interrupts generated according to alarm value
• Two alarm modes: target mode and period mode
• 52-bit target alarm value and 26-bit periodic alarm value
• Automatic reload of counter value
• Counters can be stalled if the CPU is stalled or in OCD mode
For details, see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter System Timer.
4.1.3.6
Power Management Unit
The ESP32-C3 has an advanced Power Management Unit (PMU). It can be flexibly configured to power up
different power domains of the chip to achieve the best balance between chip performance, power
consumption, and wakeup latency.
Configuring the PMU is a complex procedure. To simplify power management for typical scenarios, there are

to achieve the best balance between chip performance, power
consumption, and wakeup latency.
Configuring the PMU is a complex procedure. To simplify power management for typical scenarios, there are
the following predefined power modes that power up different combinations of power domains:
• Active mode – The CPU, RF circuits, and all peripherals are on. The chip can process data, receive,
transmit, and listen.
• Modem-sleep mode – The CPU is on, but the clock frequency can be reduced. The wireless
connections can be configured to remain active as RF circuits are periodically switched on when
required.
• Light-sleep mode – The CPU stops running, and can be optionally powered on. The chip can be woken
up via all wake up mechanisms: MAC, RTC timer, or external interrupts. Wireless connections can remain
active. Some groups of digital peripherals can be optionally shut down.
• Deep-sleep mode – Only RTC is powered on. Wireless connection data is stored in RTC memory.

Timer Group
ESP32-C3 has two 54-bit general-purpose timers, which are based on 16-bit prescalers and 54-bit
auto-reload-capable up/down-timers.
The timers’ features are summarized as follows:
• A 16-bit clock prescaler, from 1 to 65536
• A 54-bit time-base counter programmable to be incrementing or decrementing
• Able to read real-time value of the time-base counter
• Halting and resuming the time-base counter
• Programmable alarm generation
• Level interrupt generation
For details, see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter Timer Group (TIMG).
4.1.3.8
Watchdog Timers
For details, see ESP32-C3 Technical Reference Manual > Chapter Watchdog Timers.
Digital Watchdog Timers
ESP32-C3 contains three digital watchdog timers: one in each of the two timer groups (called Main System
Watchdog Timers, or MWDT) and one in the RTC module (called the RTC Watchdog Timer, or RWDT).

ESP32-C3 contains three digital watchdog timers: one in each of the two timer groups (called Main System
Watchdog Timers, or MWDT) and one in the RTC module (called the RTC Watchdog Timer, or RWDT).
During the flash boot process, RWDT and the MWDT in timer group 0 (TIMG0) are enabled automatically in
order to detect and recover from booting errors.
Digital watchdog timers have the following features:
• Four stages, each with a programmable timeout value. Each stage can be configured, enabled and
disabled separately
• Interrupt, CPU reset, or core reset for MWDT upon expiry of each stage; interrupt, CPU reset, core reset,
or system reset for RWDT upon expiry of each stage
• 32-bit expiry counter
• Write protection, to prevent RWDT and MWDT configuration from being altered inadvertently
• Flash boot protection
If the boot process from an SPI flash does not complete within a predetermined period of time, the
watchdog will reboot the entire main system.

4.3.1
Radio
This subsection describes the fundamental radio technology embedded in the chip that facilitates wireless
communication and data exchange. ESP32-C3 radio consists of the following blocks:
• 2.4 GHz receiver

4.3.1.1
2.4 GHz Receiver
The 2.4 GHz receiver demodulates the 2.4 GHz RF signal to quadrature baseband signals and converts them
to the digital domain with two high-resolution, high-speed ADCs. To adapt to varying signal channel
conditions, ESP32-C3 integrates RF filters, Automatic Gain Control (AGC), DC offset cancelation circuits, and
baseband filters.
4.3.1.2
2.4 GHz Transmitter
The 2.4 GHz transmitter modulates the quadrature baseband signals to the 2.4 GHz RF signal, and drives the

(AGC), DC offset cancelation circuits, and
baseband filters.
4.3.1.2
2.4 GHz Transmitter
The 2.4 GHz transmitter modulates the quadrature baseband signals to the 2.4 GHz RF signal, and drives the
antenna with a high-powered CMOS power amplifier. The use of digital calibration further improves the linearity
of the power amplifier.
Additional calibrations are integrated to cancel any radio imperfections, such as:
• Carrier leakage
• I/Q amplitude/phase matching
• Baseband nonlinearities
• RF nonlinearities
• Antenna matching
These built-in calibration routines reduce the cost, time, and specialized equipment required for product
testing.
4.3.1.3
Clock Generator
The clock generator produces quadrature clock signals of 2.4 GHz for both the receiver and the transmitter. All
components of the clock generator are integrated into the chip, including inductors, varactors, filters,

Functional Description
The clock generator has built-in calibration and self-test circuits. Quadrature clock phases and phase noise
are optimized on chip with patented calibration algorithms which ensure the best performance of the receiver
and the transmitter.
4.3.2
Wi-Fi
This subsection describes the chip’s Wi-Fi capabilities, which facilitate wireless communication at a high data
rate.
4.3.2.1
Wi-Fi Radio and Baseband
ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi radio and baseband support the following features:
• 802.11b/g/n
• 802.11n MCS0-7 that supports 20 MHz and 40 MHz bandwidth
• 802.11n MCS32
• 802.11n 0.4 µs guard interval
• Data rate up to 150 Mbps
• RX STBC (single spatial stream)
• Adjustable transmitting power
• Antenna diversity
ESP32-C3 supports antenna diversity with an external RF switch. This switch is controlled by one or
more GPIOs, and used to select the best antenna to minimize the effects of channel imperfections.
4.3.2.2
Wi-Fi MAC

4.3.2.2
Wi-Fi MAC
ESP32-C3 implements the full 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi MAC protocol. It supports the Basic Service Set (BSS) STA
and SoftAP operations under the Distributed Control Function (DCF). Power management is handled
automatically with minimal host interaction to minimize the active duty period.
ESP32-C3 Wi-Fi MAC applies the following low-level protocol functions automatically:
• 4 × Virtual Wi-Fi interfaces
• Infrastructure BSS in Station mode, SoftAP mode, Station + SoftAP mode, and promiscuous mode
• RTS protection, CTS protection, Immediate Block ACK
• Fragmentation and defragmentation
• TX/RX A-MPDU, TX/RX A-MSDU
• Transmit opportunity (TXOP)
• Wi-Fi multimedia (WMM)
• GCMP, CCMP, TKIP, WAPI, WEP, BIP, WPA2-PSK/WPA2-Enterprise, and WPA3-PSK/WPA3-Enterprise

4.3.2.3
Networking Features
Espressif provides libraries for TCP/IP networking, ESP-WIFI-MESH networking, and other networking

4.3.3
Bluetooth LE
This subsection describes the chip’s Bluetooth capabilities, which facilitate wireless communication for
low-power, short-range applications. ESP32-C3 includes a Bluetooth Low Energy subsystem that integrates a
hardware link layer controller, an RF/modem block and a feature-rich software protocol stack. It supports the
core features of Bluetooth 5 and Bluetooth mesh.
4.3.3.1
Bluetooth LE PHY
Bluetooth Low Energy radio and PHY in ESP32-C3 support:
• 1 Mbps PHY
• 2 Mbps PHY for higher data rates
• Coded PHY for longer range (125 Kbps and 500 Kbps)
• HW Listen before talk (LBT)

ESP32-C3 Chip Series Group Overview
ESP32-C3 Chip Series Group Overview
The ESP32-C3 chip series group is a low-power solution that provides 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11b/g/n) and
Bluetooth 5.0 connectivity, dedicated to smart home applications. This chip series group consists of the
following chip series:
• ESP32-C3 series
• ESP8685 series, a cost-down version of ESP32-C3 series
All members within the ESP32-C3 chip series group use a common set of software and reference materials,
including the technical reference manual and hardware design guidelines – See Related Documentation and
Resources.

Glossary
Glossary
chip series
A subset of chips within a chip series group with similar core features and specifications 2, 68
chip series group
A broad group of related chip products that use the same die. For example, ESP32-C3 chip series group
consists of ESP32-C3 chip series and ESP8685 chip series 2, 68
in-package flash
Flash integrated directly into the chip’s package, and external to the chip die 4, 35
off-package flash
Flash external to the chip’s package 4
peripheral
A hardware component or subsystem within the chip to interface with the outside world 16, 19
strapping pin
A type of GPIO pin used to configure certain operational settings during the chip’s power-up, and can be
reconfigured as normal GPIO after the chip’s reset 30
eFuse parameter
A parameter stored in an electrically programmable fuse (eFuse) memory within a chip. The parameter
can be set by programming EFUSE_PGM_DATAn_REG registers, and read by reading a register field
named after the parameter 30
SPI boot mode

programmable fuse (eFuse) memory within a chip. The parameter
can be set by programming EFUSE_PGM_DATAn_REG registers, and read by reading a register field
named after the parameter 30
SPI boot mode
A boot mode in which users load and execute the existing code from SPI flash 31
joint download boot mode
A boot mode in which users can download code into flash via the UART or other interfaces (see Table 3-3
Chip Boot Mode Control > Note), and load and execute the downloaded code from the flash or SRAM 31
eFuse
A one-time programmable (OTP) memory which stores system and user parameters, such as MAC
address, chip revision number, flash encryption key, etc. Value 0 indicates the default state, and value 1
indicates the eFuse has been programmed 35

Chapter 1. Introduction
This specification contains recommendations and guidelines for engineers to follow to
create modules for the expansion connectors on the NVIDIA® Jetson Orin™ Nano carrier
board. As well as understand the capabilities of the other dedicated interface
connectors and associated power solutions on the platform.
The Jetson Orin Nano carrier board is ideal for software development within the Linux
environment. Standard connectors are used to access Jetson Orin Nano features and
interfaces, enabling a highly flexible and extensible development platform. Go to
https://developer.nvidia.com/embedded/develop or r contact your NVIDIA representative
for access to software updates and the developer SDK supporting the OS image and
host development platform that you want to use. The developer SDK includes an OS
image that you will load onto your Jetson Orin Nano device, supporting documentation,

SDK supporting the OS image and
host development platform that you want to use. The developer SDK includes an OS
image that you will load onto your Jetson Orin Nano device, supporting documentation,
and code samples to help you get started.
The Jetson Orin Nano carrier board supports all the Jetson Orin Nano Series and Jetson
Orin NX Series modules.
Caution: ALWAYS CONNECT JETSON ORIN NANO and ALL EXTERNAL PERIPHERAL
DEVICES BEFORE CONNECTING THE POWER SUPPLY TO THE AC POWER JACK. Connecting
a device while powered on may damage the developer kit carrier board, Jetson Orin Nano,
or peripheral device. In addition, the carrier board should be powered down and the power
removed before plugging or unplugging devices or add-on modules into the headers. Wait
for the red power VDD_IN LED to turn off or wait for 5 minutes if your system does not
have a power LED. This includes the Jetson Orin Nano module, the camera connector, the
M.2 connector, and the other expansion headers.

The Jetson Orin Nano developer board contains ESD-sensitive parts. Always use
appropriate anti-static and grounding techniques when working with the system. Failure to
do so can result in ESD discharge to sensitive pins, and irreparably damage your Jetson Orin
Nano board. NVIDIA will not replace units that have been damaged due to ESD discharge.
Note: The developer kit carrier board has been modified to only support 5V to the module.
The MODULE_ID signal is not pulled up on the carrier board. This means that regardless of
the capability of the module, VDD_IN will be 5V only. Custom carrier boards can still be
designed to support 5V and 19V and use the MODULE_ID to identify a 5V vs. 19V Input.
Orin NX 40W (MAXN_SUPER) is NOT supported on the developer kit carrier board.

Chapter 2. Jetson Nano Carrier Board
Standard Connectors
The Jetson Orin Nano carrier board provides several connectors with industry standard
pinouts to support additional functionality beyond what is integrated on the main
platform board. This includes:
> USB 3.2: Type C connector
> USB 3.2: 2 x Type A stacked connectors
> Gigabit Ethernet: RJ45 connector
> DisplayPort connector
> M.2, Key E socket
> M.2, Key M socket (4-lane PCIe)
> M.2, Key M socket (2-lane PCIe)
2.1
USB Ports
The carrier board supports five USB connectors. One is a USB 3.2 Type C connector (J5)
supporting host, device, and USB Recovery. In addition, there are two, dual stacked USB
3.2 Type A connectors (J6 and J7). Each connector supports host mode only. A load
switch supplying VBUS is provided for each of the USB 3.2 ports per stack and is limited
to 3A of output current.

and I2C optional.

The Jetson Orin Nano carrier board includes a M.2, Key E Slot Mini-PCIe Expansion slot
(J10). This includes interface options for WiFi/BT including PCIe (x1), USB 2.0, UART, I2S,

R106 and R107. Care should be taken as some M.2 cards can cause conflicts with other
devices connected to the I2C interface.

3.3
40-Pin Expansion Header
The Jetson Orin Nano carrier board includes a 40-pin (2x20, 2.54 mm pitch) expansion
header (J12). The connector used on the carrier board is an Astron Technology (Part #
27-0169H-220-1G-H).
The expansion connector includes various audio and control interfaces including:
> I2S
> Audio (AU) clock
> I2C (x2)
> SPI (x2)
> UART
> GPIOs (x3 – See notes)
Notes:
>
All the signals on the expansion header use 3.3V levels.
>
All the interface signal pins (I2S, I2C, SPI, UART, and AU clock) can also be configured as
GPIOs.
>
Any pull-up or pull-down resistors on the signals (except I2C) must be weak (limited to
>50 kΩ).

Overview
The BTS 7960 is part of the NovalithIC family containing three separate chips in one
package: One p-channel highside MOSFET and one n-channel lowside MOSFET
together with a driver IC, forming a fully integrated high current half-bridge. All three
chips are mounted on one common leadframe, using the chip on chip and chip by chip
technology. The power switches utilize vertical MOS technologies to ensure optimum on
state resistance. Due to the p-channel highside switch the need for a charge pump is
eliminated thus minimizing EMI. Interfacing to a microcontroller is made easy by the
integrated driver IC which features logic level inputs, diagnosis with current sense, slew
rate adjustment, dead time generation and protection against overtemperature,
overvoltage, undervoltage, overcurrent and short circuit. The BTS 7960 can be

The power stages of the BTS 7960 consist of a p-channel vertical DMOS transistor for
the high side switch and a n-channel vertical DMOS transistor for the low side switch. All
protection and diagnostic functions are located in a separate top chip. Both switches can
be operated up to 25 kHz, allowing active freewheeling and thus minimizing power
dissipation in the forward operation of the integrated diodes.

4.3
Protection Functions
The device provides integrated protection functions. These are designed to prevent IC
destruction under fault conditions described in the data sheet. Fault conditions are
considered as “outside” normal operating range. Protection functions are not to be used
for continuous or repetitive operation, with the exception of the current limitation
(Chapter 4.3.4). In a fault condition the BTS 7960 will apply the highest slew rate
possible independent of the connected slew rate resistor. Overvoltage, overtemperature
and overcurrent are indicated by a fault current IIS(LIM) at the IS pin as described in the
paragraph “Status Flag Diagnosis With Current Sense Capability” on Page 17 and
Figure 10.
In the following the protection functions are listed in order of their priority. Overvoltage
lock out overrides all other error modes.
4.3.1
Overvoltage Lock Out

Figure 10.
In the following the protection functions are listed in order of their priority. Overvoltage
lock out overrides all other error modes.
4.3.1
Overvoltage Lock Out
To assure a high immunity against overvoltages (e.g. load dump conditions) the device
shuts the lowside MOSFET off and turns the highside MOSFET on, if the supply voltage
is exceeding the over voltage protection level VOV(OFF). The IC operates in normal mode
again with a hysteresis VOV(HY) if the supply voltage decreases below the switch-on
voltage VOV(ON). In H-bridge configuration, this behavior of the BTS 7960 will lead to
freewheeling in highside during over voltage.
4.3.2
Undervoltage Shut Down
To avoid uncontrolled motion of the driven motor at low voltages the device shuts off
(output is tri-state), if the supply voltage drops below the switch-off voltage VUV(OFF). The
IC becomes active again with a hysteresis VUV(HY) if the supply voltage rises above the
switch-on voltage VUV(ON).

tri-state), if the supply voltage drops below the switch-off voltage VUV(OFF). The
IC becomes active again with a hysteresis VUV(HY) if the supply voltage rises above the
switch-on voltage VUV(ON).
4.3.3
Overtemperature Protection
The BTS 7960 is protected against overtemperature by an integrated temperature
sensor. Overtemperature leads to a shut down of both output stages. This state is
latched until the device is reset by a low signal with a minimum length of treset at the INH
pin, provided that its temperature has decreased at least the thermal hysteresis ∆T in the
meantime.
Repetitive use of the overtemperature protection might reduce lifetime.
4.3.4

4.4
Control and Diagnostics
4.4.1
Input Circuit
The control inputs IN and INH consist of TTL/CMOS compatible schmitt triggers with
hysteresis which control the integrated gate drivers for the MOSFETs. Setting the INH
pin to high enables the device. In this condition one of the two power switches is switched
on depending on the status of the IN pin. To deactivate both switches, the INH pin has
to be set to low. No external driver is needed. The BTS 7960 can be interfaced directly
to a microcontroller.
4.4.2
Dead Time Generation
In bridge applications it has to be assured that the highside and lowside MOSFET are
not conducting at the same time, connecting directly the battery voltage to GND. This is
assured by a circuit in the driver IC, generating a so called dead time between switching
off one MOSFET and switching on the other. The dead time generated in the driver IC is

4.4.3
Adjustable Slew Rate
In order to optimize electromagnetic emission, the switching speed of the MOSFETs is
adjustable by an external resistor. The slew rate pin SR allows the user to optimize the
balance between emission and power dissipation within his own application by
connecting an external resistor RSR to GND.
4.4.4
Status Flag Diagnosis With Current Sense Capability
The status pin IS is used as a combined current sense and error flag output. In normal
operation (current sense mode), a current source is connected to the status pin, which
delivers a current proportional to the forward load current flowing through the active high
side switch. If the high side switch is inactive or the current is flowing in the reverse

status pin, which

direction no current will be driven except for a marginal leakage current IIS(LK). The

value of 8500 for the current sense ratio kILIS = IL / IIS, a resistor value of RIS = 1kΩ leads
to VIS = (IL / 8.5 A)V. In case of a fault condition the status output is connected to a

Layout Considerations
Due to the fast switching times for high currents, special care has to be taken to the PCB
layout. Stray inductances have to be minimized in the power bridge design as it is
necessary in all switched high power bridges. The BTS 7960 has no separate pin for
power ground and logic ground. Therefore it is recommended to assure that the offset
between the ground connection of the slew rate resistor, the current sense resistor and
ground pin of the device (GND / pin 1) is minimized. If the BTS 7960 is used in a H-bridge
or B6 bridge design, the voltage offset between the GND pins of the different devices
should be small as well.

current for the switching phase via a low inductance path and therefore reducing noise
and ground bounce. A reasonable value for this capacitor would be about 470 nF.
